It is a simple structure with almost no decorations, {{ill|lt=gabled structure|Q13308575|qid=Q13308575|1=Kirizuma-style}}, and both have a 2-ken gable roof and a 2-ken girder, but the Tosetsu-sha has a 2-ken girder and the Sai-setsu-sha has a 3-ken length. Ryosetsusha was also rebuilt at the same time as the main shrine. Each has a gabled roofed roof with a flat thatched roof, and the roofed roof is designated as a cultural property by Kyoto Prefecture. * Saisetsha ** Deities enshrined: Kumano Shrine in Kuroda, Wakamiya Shrine in {{ill|lt=Yokota, Sonobe Town|Q131900099|qid=Q131900099|lt=Yokota|1=Yokota}}, |Miwa Shrine, Kamo Shrine in Omura, Shishi Sugahara Shrine, Handa Omori Shrine ** Enshrined on the right hand side facing the main shrine. See Tosetsha. * Shu Shrine * Kotohira Shrine * Sanno Shrine * Inari Shrine * {{ill|lt=Ise Jingu|Q687168|qid=Q687168|1=Ise Grand Shrine}} Far place of worship * Outside company ** {{ill|lt=Otabisho|Q11489117|qid=Q11489117|1=Otabisho}} ({{Wiki coordinates|35|6|22.93|N|135|26|20.23|E|region:JP|Yawata Shrine|name=Yawata Shrine ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Otabisho|1=UNKNOWN}})}}, Funasaka, Sonobe-cho, Nantan City) [https://tanbarakuichi.sakura.ne.jp/shrine/sonobe/04.html#s036 Hachiman Shrine] (Tamba Shrine [Personal Site]) Make-jinja otabisho.JPG|Otabisho (Hachiman Shrine) === Ritual organization === === Shinto priest === Engi's receipts suggest that a yubu was established during the Heian period, but the details are unknown. From the Middle Ages to the early modern period, Godaisan Takinji Temple was in charge as a Betto, and after the temple was abolished, the Ueda clan, a descendant of the Sonobe clan, took over the position of chief priest. === Miyaza === In each hamlet (village) of shrine parishioners, a group called ``Miyashu'' (Miyashu), which is made up of influential ``byo'' ({{ill|lt=surname|Q69634220|qid=Q69634220|lt=surname|1=myōji}}) of the clan group called ``kabu'', is organized, and they participate in festivals and perform their respective divine duties. In the case of Takei, the Miyamoto, one Miyashu is selected from each of the six specific families of the former {{ill|lt=Maki Village|Q30938084|qid=Q30938084|1=Make}} (term of six years). . From the other former Shinoda, Imai, and Tsujita families, eight specific families assumed the position of chief priest (kujuto, kunyuto). , assisting the chief priest in rituals, etc. The Miyaza of each of these villages is responsible for the rituals of the Moki Shrine, and at the same time is also involved in the rituals of the respective village ujigami, and there is a multilayered structure in which the rituals of the village ujigami and the rituals of the main ujigami, the Magi Shrine, are recognized. This multilayered structure of rituals is widely recognized in the Tamba region, and the rituals at Maki Shrine can be considered a typical example of this because of the breadth of the area and the preservation of the ancient style of Shinto rituals. ; Multilayered structure of ritualsFor example, in the case of Shimo-shin-e Village, there is a group of Okanae and 7 other members of the same family, and 5 of these members form the shrine sect called {{ill|lt=Toya|UNKNOWN|lt=Toya system}}, and at the same time they serve the Shinko Festival and are also responsible for the rituals of Hiruko Shrine, the village's guardian deity, which also overlaps with the rituals of the Kuta, which enshrines the ancestral deity. The Okabu family is said to be a descendant of a medieval {{ill|lt=jiji-samurai|Q13432011|qid=Q13432011|1=Jizamurai}}, and behind the main family's mansion there is a {{ill|lt=spring water|Q1881858|qid=Q1881858|1=spring water}} called ``Morisan Water'' and a small shrine called ``Jishu Daigongen'' enshrined as deities of the stock, which are the original ``guardian deities.'' Similarly, other stocks enshrined stock deities (mostly large trees) called ``Morisan'', ``Jigami'', and ``Yama no Kami'' on a per-plant basis, and together with other stocks, they formed shrines and took part in the rituals at Ebisu-jinja Shrine and Maki-jinja Shrine. In this way, each village in the ``Eleven Villages'' has three layers of overlapping rituals: ``Ushigami,'' ``Village Ujigami,'' and ``General Ujigami.'' Similarly, in Takei, which is a Miyamoto province, the Maki Shrine, which is the general guardian deity, is also regarded as the village guardian deity, but the rituals are divided into three parts: those of the ``village guardian deity'' and those of the ``general guardian deity.'' === Main festivals === === Rice planting festival === The rice-planting festival is a ritual to celebrate the fertility of {{ill|lt=Gokoku|Q1191138|qid=Q1191138|1=Five Grains}} of the Takei village, which represents the character of the deity enshrined at this shrine.In early modern times, it was held on May 5th ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Boys' Festival|1=UNKNOWN}}), but due to the calendar change, it was held on June 5th, and now it is held on the Sunday closest to June 5th. First, {{ill|lt=food for the gods|Q11591045|qid=Q11591045|1=Shinsen}} and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=rice cake|1=UNKNOWN}} were offered, and {{ill|lt=oryoto|Q1760119|qid=Q1760119|1=Norito}} was played, and then {{ill|lt=taiko|Q11404|qid=Q11404|1=Drum}} was placed in the shrine. {{ill|lt=Saotome|Q539854|qid=Q539854|1=Saotome}} wearing {{ill|lt=kasuri|Q3081545|qid=Q3081545|1=Kasuri}} of {{ill|lt=cotton|Q11457|qid=Q11457|1=Cotton}} of nk|indigo dye|Q11622590}} form a circle and dance the ``rice planting dance'' to the beat of the drum and songs. Next, the head of the shrine (see the previous section) holds a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=bamboo pole|1=UNKNOWN}} with a house-shaped board attached to the tip and a {{ill|lt=naruko (instrument)|UNKNOWN|lt=naruko}} suspended from it, as if it were a {{ill|lt=hoe|Q131154|qid=Q131154|1=Hoe (tool)}}, and performs the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=paddling|1=UNKNOWN}} gesture, using the stairs (5 steps) of the main shrine as a rice field. Afterwards, the two Saotomes are handed 25 sacred rice cakes by the chief priest, and each of them makes the gesture of planting five rice cakes on each step of the stairs, which are made to look like rice fields (the rice cakes are likened to seedlings). Next, the ``Rice Planting Dance'' is repeated, and when it is finished, Saotome collects the rice cakes she has planted and hands them over to the chief priest again, and the worshipers complete the ritual by offering {{ill|lt=Tamagushi|Q7680557|qid=Q7680557|1=Tamagushi}}.It is said that in ancient times, {{ill|lt=kagura|Q1348260|qid=Q1348260|1=Kagura}} was performed by {{ill|lt=priestess|Q1047139|qid=Q1047139|1=Miko}}, but the details are unknown. The current "rice planting dance" was created by the chief priest at the time in {{ill|lt=Showa|Q327567|qid=Q327567|1=Shōwa era}}9 ({{ill|lt=1934|Q18714|qid=Q18714|1=1934}})[http://www.bunkashisan.ne.jp/search/ViewContent.php?from=14&ContentID=135 Regional Cultural Asset Portal, ``Maki Shrine Rice Planting Festival''] (accessed October 26, 2010). The "Rice-planting Dance" was created in 1923 during {{ill|lt=Emperor Showa|Q34479|qid=Q34479|1=Hirohito}}'s {{ill|lt=Daijosai|Q11433653|qid=Q11433653|1=Daijosai}}. The song is said to have been written and choreographed based on the rice-planting ceremony that took place when the area around {{ill|lt=Ogami Shrine|Q11488762|qid=Q11488762|1=Mikami Shrine}} in 1358}} was designated as Yukida. , although it belongs to a new category, the rest remains well preserved. In addition, many women from the shrine parishioners participated in the "Rice Planting Dance", but that organization was disbanded in {{ill|lt=postwar|Q1201472|qid=Q1201472|1=Post-war}}, and in 1975 ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=1975|1=UNKNOWN}}), the number of women participating has decreased, so in August 1981, the God-Respecting Women's Association was formed to maintain and pass on the tradition, and since then, 10 to 15 people, mainly from the association, have been participating in the "Rice Planting Dance.". === Shinko Festival === The Shinko Festival is a festival of the 11 villages (11 shrines) of Makigo, and in early modern times, it was held from August {{ill|lt=last day|Q4704589|qid=Q4704589|1=misoka}} to September {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=first day|1=UNKNOWN}} along with the regular festival. Since Meiji 16 ({{ill|lt=1883|Q7816|qid=Q7816|1=1883}}), the Shinko Festival has been held on October 14th and 15th, but since {{ill|lt=Heisei|Q234510|qid=Q234510|1=Heisei era}} 15th year ({{ill|lt=2003|Q1986|qid=Q1986|1=2003}}), the Shinko Festival has been held on the third Saturday and Sunday of October. In the past, in addition to Miyamoto, parishioners from 9 villages and 11 companies participated, but currently the 4 villages of Kuroda, {{ill|lt=Yokota, Sonobe Town|Q131900099|qid=Q131900099|lt=Yokota|1=Yokota}}, Omura, and Kuchihatta do not participate. . ; the previous day On the day before the Shinko Festival, a shrine was set up in the gardens of the shrine inns set up in Funasaka and Nie.In the past, in Funasaka, the shrine was chosen from among the 12 designated families, and later from the house of the group on duty (in some cases, newly built houses were selected) (``Shikiuchisha Survey Report''). The chief priest of this shrine visits Funasaka, and the chief priest (see the previous section) visits Nie to prepare for the festival. ; 1st dayEarly on the morning of the day, two messengers from the Shishi people were sent to our shrine, and after a festival (Shishi people offering ceremony) was held where sake and {{ill|lt=edamame|Q1377879|qid=Q1377879|1=Edamame}} were offered, the shrine was again {{ill|lt=morning|Q55313888|qid=Q55313888|1=a.m.}}1 The festival begins at 0:00, and at 2:00 PM, the {{ill|lt=Mikoshi|Q979940|qid=Q979940|1=Mikoshi}} departs for {{ill|lt=Otabisho|Q11489117|qid=Q11489117|1=Otabisho}} in Funasaka, and the Shinko Festival begins. On the way, the mikoshi is greeted by a {{ill|lt=chigo|Q30940647|qid=Q30940647|1=Chigo}} procession from Nie and heads to Ebisu Shrine, where it is enshrined in the hall of worship and undergoes rituals by the head of the shrine and Nie's members of the shrine (see the previous section) before heading back to the otabisho. Then, a procession of Chigo from Funasaka joins them on the way, arrives at the Otabisho in the evening, the mikoshi is placed in a temporary hall set up at the Otabisho, and receives an offering of {{ill|lt=Tawara|Q11386402|qid=Q11386402|1=tawara}} containing fresh grain from Nie and Funasaka. Regarding Chigo, Nie is considered to be a female character, and Funasaka is considered to be a male character, and they are required to wear either female or male costumes. Until around 1932, a similar mikoshi was carried from Wakamiya Shrine in {{ill|lt=Yokota, Sonobe-machi|Q131900099|qid=Q131900099|lt=Yokota|1=Yokota}}, and people from Funasaka would meet them and accompany them to Otabisho, where the mikoshi of both Moki and Wakamiya shrines would be lined up and lodged together. ; 2nd dayIn the early hours of the next morning (around 2 a.m.), shrine parishioners including the Takei, Nie, Funasaka, Shishi, Onishi, and Handa shrines gather at the otabisho, where ``neri'' and dedications of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=sumo power|1=UNKNOWN}} are held. At this time, a person called Satanin, chosen from among the Shishi and Onishi, performs the ritual under the instructions of the chief priest.The Satanin of the Shishi is changed every other year, and the Satanin of the Onishi is changed every year. . First, the ritual begins with the command from the Sata people to ``offer the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=sacred sake|1=UNKNOWN}},'' and the worshipers chosen from Funasaka hold the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=sakaki|1=UNKNOWN}} in their mouths and bring two {{ill|lt=bottles|Q3129558|qid=Q3129558|1=heishi}} filled with the sacred sake to the shrine. Next, pour it into {{ill|lt=Choshi|Q2972145|qid=Q2972145|1=Chōshi}} and give it to the chief priest who attends the shrine. The priest who receives it refills it into another bottle and offers it, and the Choshi returns it to the donor. Next, when the Sataman commands, ``Drop the sacred sake,'' the chief priest pours the sacred sake from the bottle into the {{ill|lt=cup|Q3469363|qid=Q3469363|1=sakazuki}}, leaves it in front of the shrine, and returns the remaining sacred sake, along with the bottle, to the donor. Next, Satajin tells the chief priest, ``Come and enjoy the sacred sake,'' and together they go down to the gathering hall in the otabisho called ``Funasakacho,'' where they perform {{ill|lt=direct meeting|Q11581721|qid=Q11581721|1=Naorai}} with divine sake and a side dish made from cut {{ill|lt=persimmons|Q29526|qid=Q29526|1=Persimmon}}. Afterwards, the chief priest and Satato returned to the shrine again, and Satato ordered them to "stand for the offering," and the offeror gave two large {{ill|lt=笥|Q11600004|qid=Q11600004|1=ke}} offerings to the god. Eleven bowls and small bowls of sacred food are offered (the large bowl is said to be for the deity enshrined at this shrine, and the small bowl is said to be for the deity enshrined at the Setsusha (the deity enshrined at the Setsusha is also the deity enshrined at the 11 guardian deities of each village)), and the process begins. It is said that at the time when the mikoshi of Wakamiya Shrine lived together in the same lodging, the dedicator divided into two groups and carried the offerings to each mikoshi, and the shrine maiden from Wakamiya Shrine received the offerings and offered them to the mikoshi. Although it is now abbreviated, in the past, before the parade, the food was withdrawn with the signal of ``Sata-oroshi'' from the Sata people.The neri is also called ``doronai tori'' because of the way it is performed, and it is performed by Satato, Takei, and Handa's kakurikitori. The performer picks up a sword for one person, hangs a fish basket around his waist, and goes around the {{ill|lt=dohyō|Q832429|qid=Q832429|1=Dohyō}} set up in the Otabisho once.During this, he stabs the ground with his sword and says things like ``Ottaa'' while grabbing a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=doronago|1=UNKNOWN}} and making a gesture to put it in the fish basket. Afterwards, the head of the shrine calls for a sumo force, but first the actual action is performed, followed by what is called ``half sumo force.'' The fights are divided into ``Dekaku Riki'' and ``Machikaku Riki'', with the Kakuro Tori of the Machikaku Riki-ka going up to the ring first and receiving techniques from the Dekaku Riki-ka who comes up later, and the 7th match being held with the Dekaku Riki-ka playing the winning role and the Machikaku Riki-ka playing the losing role (however, there is no winner or loser). Half-force power is when one person performs the act of taking power (one-person power), and at the end, the person rolls around as if he has been thrown away. This represents the opponent of the rice spirit, an invisible god of energy, and by being thrown away by that god, it is said to be a blessing to the gods and a prayer for a bountiful harvest. Once the half-witness force is finished, Takei and Funasaka perform the training, and the ritual ends. It is customary for parishioners from 11 shrines to participate in the ceremony, and in the four villages that are not participating, members of Takei serve as substitutes to maintain the ancient status. Regarding the practice, it seems to be a remnant of the past negative attitude (Makewaza) associated with the power of power with the gods due to its humorous appearance, but it is considered to be a tradition that should be considered along with the ``Catfish Osame Shinto Ritual'' handed down at Ishigami Shrine in {{ill|lt=Hyogo Prefecture|Q130290|qid=Q130290|1=Hyōgo Prefecture}}.Around 2:00 pm on the second day of the Shinko Festival, the parishioners gather together bringing items such as straw bags, {{ill|lt=bow and arrows|Q19827042|qid=Q19827042|1=Bow and arrow}}, targets, {{ill|lt=floor boxes|Q11485954|qid=Q11485954|1=Shogi}}, and orihito. First, the people from Funasaka offered bales and orihito to the mikoshi, and after singing prayers, Nie and Funasaka's party, led by Satato, offered {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=bundles|1=UNKNOWN}}, bows, targets, bales, orihito, etc., and the Shishi and Onishi on duty {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=plow|1=UNKNOWN}} - Two {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=machiko|1=UNKNOWN}} {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=cow|1=UNKNOWN}} carrying {{ill|lt=horse hoe|Q209042|qid=Q209042|1=Harrow (tool)}} follow in a single line and circle around the Funasaka Office three times in a thousand degrees. At the end of Osendo, children from Nie and Funasaka wave bundles of money in front of the mikoshi (hohei), and then a Yabusame ceremony is held in which they ride on {{ill|lt=wooden horse|Q647794|qid=Q647794|1=Rocking horse}} and shoot arrows at targets held up by the target bearer.Yabusame used to be held early in the morning (``Shikinaisha Investigation Report''). . Once Yabusame is over, the mikoshi is returned to the shrine. After Kanko left the Otabisho, everyone other than Takei and Nie saw the mikoshi off to Sasayama Kaido, and Nie's group accompanied him to the vicinity of Nie's community center. When the mikoshi returns to Maki Shrine in the evening, the festival ends by carrying it around the shrine, shaking it vigorously up and down. Furthermore, until 1962 (1962|Q2764}}), mikoshis were carried on pilgrimages, but due to the decrease in the number of people carrying them, they are now carried on carts. === Cultural assets === === Cultural property designated by Kyoto Prefecture === *Tangible cultural property ** Maki Shrine 3 buildings (buildings) - Designated on April 14, 1984 [http://www.kyoto-be.ne.jp/bunkazai/cms/?page_id=200 Kyoto Prefecture designated/registered cultural properties] (Kyoto Prefecture Board of Education). . *** Main shrine *** Tosetsha *** Saisetsha *** (Designated) 3 covered houses === Kyoto prefecture registered cultural property === *Tangible cultural property ** Maki Shrine 3 buildings (buildings) - Registered on April 14, 1984. *** Emasha *** Shinmon *** Torii === Kyoto Prefecture Cultural Properties Environmental Conservation District === * Maki Shrine Cultural Properties Environmental Conservation District - Decided on April 14, 1984. === Cultural property designated by Nantan City === * Natural monument ** Tengu cedar at the mouth of Maki Shrine - Designated on April 13, 2017 {{PDFlink|[http://www.be.city.nantan.kyoto.jp/syakaikyouiku/bunkazai29.6.8.pdf Nantan City Cultural Properties List]}} (Nantan City homepage). . === Local information === ; Location * {{ill|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|Q120730|qid=Q120730|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Nantan City|Q170421|qid=Q170421|1=Nantan, Kyoto}}3 Takei Miyanoya, Sonobe Town ; Transportation access * bus ** {{ill|lt=Sonobe Station|Q1044120|qid=Q1044120|1=Sonobe Station}} ({{ill|lt=West Japan Railway Company|Q502125|qid=Q502125|lt=JR West|1=West Japan Railway Company}}{{ill|lt=Sagano Line|Q1073011|qid=Q1073011|1=Sagano Line}}/{{ill|lt=San'in Main Line|Q1135170|qid=Q1135170|1=San'in Main Line}}), take the Nantan Municipal Bus (44 Enshino Line) and get off at the "Makijinja-mae" bus stop. (About 5 minutes walk after getting off) * car ** Parking: Yes ; around * Mt. Takinji - the mountain behind the temple grounds * {{ill|lt=Kuhonji Temple (Nantan City)|Q11370081|qid=Q11370081|lt=Kuhonji Temple|1=Kubon-ji Temple}} === Footnotes === {{Footnote help}} {{Reflist|2}} === References === * “Shikinaisha Research Report” edited by Shikinaisha Research Association, Volume 18, Sanin-do 1, Kogakukan University Publishing Department, 1988. * Yukinori Ueki "Maki Shrine" (Kenichi Tanigawa ed. "Japanese Gods - Shrines and Sacred Sites - 7 San'in" ({{ill|lt=Hakusuisha|Q4346470|qid=Q4346470|1=Hakusuisha Publishing}}, 1985) ISBN 4-560-02217-8) * “Sonobe Town History Comprehensive Edition Illustrated History of Sonobe”, Sonobe Town/Sonobe Town Board of Education, 2005 * “Japanese Historical Place Name System: Place Names of Kyoto Prefecture” ({{ill|lt=Heibonsha|Q11482108|qid=Q11482108|1=Heibonsha}}) Funai District Maki Shrine section === External link === {{Commons category|Make-jinja}} * [http://21coe.kokugakuin.ac.jp/db/jinja/360202.html Asaki Shrine] (Kokugakuin University 21st Century COE Program “Shinto and Shrine Historical Materials Collection”) * [http://www.bunkashisan.ne.jp/search/ViewContent.php?from=14&ContentID=135 Maki Shrine Rice Planting Festival] (Regional Creation Foundation, "Regional Cultural Asset Portal") {{Shinto horizontal}} == Categories == [[Category:Wikidata generated shikinaisha pages|Make Shrine (Q11498617)]][[Category:Shikinaisha|Make Shrine (Q11498617)]][[Category:Shikinaisha|Make Shrine (Q11498617)]][[Category:Shikinaisha in Tanba Province]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Kyoto Prefecture]] [[Category:History of Nantan, Kyoto]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Tanba Province|名まけしんしや]] [[Category:Former Fu-sha in Kyoto]] [[Category:Sonobe Domain]] [[Category:Buildings and structures in Nantan, Kyoto]]

Shinko festival (third Saturday and Sunday in October) |Map = {{Location map|Japan Kyoto|label=Maki Shrine|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}}{{maplink2|frame=yes|plain=yes|type=point|zoom=11|marker=religious-shinto|frame-align=center|frame-width=200|frame-height=200}} }} ``Make Shrine'' is located in Takei, Sonobe Town, {{ill|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|Q120730|qid=Q120730|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Nantan City|Q170421|qid=Q170421|1=Nantan, Kyoto}}. {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shikinaisha|1=Shikinaisha|qid=Q134917286}} ({{ill|lt=Meishin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964|1=Myōjin Taisha}}) and {{ill|lt=Modern shrine rank system|Q712534|qid=Q712534|lt=Old shrine rank|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}} is {{ill|UNKNOWN|qid=Q134917326|lt=Fusha|1=Fu-sha}}. === Overview === It is located at the westernmost tip of Sonobe-cho, Nantan City, facing north at the northern foot of Mt. Takintera. Since early modern times, it has been referred to as the ``general guardian of the 11 villages of Makigo'' as a common {{ill|lt=tutelary deity|Q767655|qid=Q767655|1=Ujigami}} of the surrounding villages along the Sasayama Highway, including Takei Village, which is the Miyamoto (shrine). The main hall, Tosetsha Shrine, and Saisetsha Shrine, which are enshrined within a thatched roof, are cultural properties designated by Kyoto Prefecture, and the precincts have been designated as a Kyoto Prefecture Cultural Property Environmental Conservation District. Because of its charm, it is often used as a filming location for period dramas filmed in Kyoto. Furthermore, ``Japanese Gods'' is also known as the only shrine in the Tanba region whose main building faces north. According to the shrine's legend, it is the only Kitamen Shrine in the Tamba region, but there are other examples such as {{ill|lt=So Shrine|Q11452023|qid=Q11452023|1=Sō Shrine (Nantan)}}. . === Enshrined God === * '''Omiketsuhiko no Mikoto'' :: Another name for {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Amagoyane no Mikoto|1=UNKNOWN}}'s {{ill|lt=Mikogami|Q352176|qid=Q352176|1=Mikogami}} and {{ill|lt=Amagoyune no Mikoto|Q91088537|qid=Q91088537|1=Ame-no-Oshikumone}}, and is said to be the god that controls water and food. Regarding the enshrined deity, there is a different theory that suggests that it is Oomiketsuhime no Mikoto (Oomiketsuhime no Mikoto, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ogitsuhime|1=UNKNOWN}}), such as in Enkei Deguchi's ``{{ill|lt=Shinmeichō Kosho|Q11588824|qid=Q11588824|1=Engishiki Jinmyōchō Studies}}''. . In addition, the shrine's name "Make" is thought to have come from the word "mike" (food), and the current Shinto ritual {{ill|lt=Otaue Festival|Q11489226|qid=Q11489226|lt=Ocean Festival|1=Otaue Festival}} is said to be a god deeply involved in agriculture. Because of this, it is thought to be the food god (Miketsukami) who presides over food. name="Investigation report">``Shikiuchi company investigation report''. . Furthermore, due to the location of the enshrinement site, it has been pointed out that Mt. The × marks are villages that originally did not participate. |-| style="font-size:1.2em; background-color:white; border-right-color:white; border-bottom-color:white; border-left-color:white;" colspan="8" | {{List of coordinates|Section=General guardianship of the eleven villages of Makigo}} |} In the early modern period, in addition to Takei Village, which was Miyamoto, it was considered the joint deity of neighboring villages. , Funasaka (Funasaka, Sonobe Town), Onishi (Onishi, Sonobe Town), Shishiudo (Shishito, Sonobe Town), Handa (Handa, Sonobe Town), Kuroda (Kuroda, Sonobe Town), {{ill|lt=Sonbe Town Side田|Q131900099|qid=Q131900099|lt=Yokota|1=Yokota}} (Yokota, Sonobe Town), Omura (Jonan Town, Sonobe Town), Kuchihatta ({{jalink|Kyotanba Town|Q1203236} }It refers to the 11 villages of Kuchito (Kuchito, Sonobe Town), Koshi (Koshi, Sonobe Town).Kuchito and Koshi Village are excluded when it is said to be the ``total guardian of the 11 villages of Makigo.'' It was also called ``the total guardian of ''.In terms of village units in the early modern period, Takei Village in Miyamoto was divided into three villages, Shinoda, Maki, and Kaminoine (Kamishinoe Village was further divided into two villages, Imai and Tsujita when it came to festivals at this shrine ), and other villages were also divided into multiple villages, with a total of 19 villages having total guardianship (see the table on the right). Although it does not correspond to the name ``Eleven Villages,'' there were a total of 11 shrines in the parish village of our shrine, and they were positioned as subsidiary shrines of our shrine. Therefore, in this case, the term ``Soshinju of the 11 villages'' means the guardian deities of the 11 shrines. Furthermore, the town name ``Makikyo'' cannot be confirmed in historical sources, so it is thought to be a regional common name, but since the area of ​​rituals was spread out over the surrounding villages, which gives it a very medieval appearance, it can be assumed that it was a wide-area name dating back to the Middle Ages. One proof of this is that even though this area was divided into the {{ill|lt=Sonobe clan|Q10863377|qid=Q10863377|lt=Sonobe|1=Sonobe Domain}} and {{ill|lt=Tamba Kameyama clan|Q10854981|qid=Q10854981|lt=Kameyama|1=Tanba-Kameyama Domain}} clans during the feudal period, they were jointly in charge of rituals, transcending the boundaries of the feudal government. === History === === Outline === The year of establishment is unknown. {{jalink|Daido included in "{{ill|lt=Shinsho Kokufusho|Q11502312|qid=Q11502312|1=Shinshō Kyakuchokufushō}}" (Japan)|Q1373191|Datong}} in {{ill|lt=牒|Q11569993|qid=Q11569993|1=chō}} in the first year ({{ill|lt=806|Q30021|qid=Q30021|1=806}}) of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Jingo Keiun|1=UNKNOWN}}4 ({{ill|lt=770|Q25021|qid=Q25021|1=770}}), indicating that rituals were being held at that time. It is said that when it was first founded, it was located at the foot of a mountain further back than its current location, and was moved to its current location due to landslides caused by heavy rains and for the convenience of worshipers. However, there are no records left to prove this, including the date. Around the enshrinement site, there are {{ill|lt=kofun|Q1141225|qid=Q1141225|1=Kofun}} scattered around, including the Yasutani kofun group of Kuchiudo, Sonobe town, as well as land where old coins were found, indicating that this area was an open land from an early time.{{ill|lt=Renju|Q1373077|qid=Q1373077|1=Ninju}}2nd year ({{ill|lt=852 years|Q30383|qid=Q30383|1=852}}), {{ill|lt=Emmissary|Q11399920|qid=Q11399920|1=Chokushi}} was sent and {{ill|lt=hohei|Q11445508|qid=Q11445508|1=Hōhei}} was made in "{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Emperor Montoku's True Record|1=UNKNOWN}}" article on Koshin (12th) of November of the same year. . However, it is thought that it gradually declined after that.In the {{ill|lt=Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963|1=Edo period}}, it was revered by the {{ill|lt=Koide clan|Q11459112|qid=Q11459112|1=Koide clan (Negi Daibu)}}, the lord of the {{ill|lt=Sonobe domain|Q10863377|qid=Q10863377|1=Sonobe Domain}}, and was restored. link|Genroku|Q1325001|During the Genroku era}} (end of the 17th century), domain funds were used to repair the main shrine, rebuild and construct the worship hall, tower gate, stone torii gate, etc. Also, it was designated as the {{ill|lt=prayer place|Q11588473|qid=Q11588473|1=Kigan-sho}} of the Koide clan, where the lord of the domain visited directly or on his behalf, and Takinji Temple was designated as {{ill|lt=Bettoji|Q11396755|qid=Q11396755|1=Bettō-ji}} ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=main temple|1=UNKNOWN}} is Kuhonji Temple). On the evening of December 18, 1762, Horeki 11 ({{ill|lt=1762|Q7652|qid=Q7652|1=1762}}), an accidental fire from the {{ill|lt=kuri|Q3078145|qid=Q3078145|1=Kuri (kitchen)}} of Takinji Temple, which was nearby, spread and the entire precincts, including the shrine, were almost completely destroyed, and ancient records and treasures were also lost. Reconstruction of the shrine began in Horeki 14 ({{ill|lt=1764|Q7659|qid=Q7659|1=1764}}), with the help of the feudal lord {{ill|lt=Hidemochi Koide|Q11459132|qid=Q11459132|1=Koide Fusayoshi}} and Mr. It was completed in July of {{ill|lt=Meiwa|Q1146161|qid=Q1146161|1=Meiwa}}4 ({{ill|lt=1767|Q7672|qid=Q7672|1=1767}}) with a donation from his son|Q125562175}} (current main hall, etc.).With the {{ill|lt=Meiji period|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096|1=Meiji era}} {{ill|lt=separation of Shinto and Buddhism|Q1970535|qid=Q1970535|1=Shinbutsu bunri}}, Betto Takinji Temple was abolished, and the temple's fixtures were inherited by the shrine. , in the same year ({{ill|lt=1873|Q7757|qid=Q7757|1=1873}}), it was ranked as {{ill|lt=gosha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316|1=Gō-sha}} in {{ill|lt=modern shrine rank system|Q712534|qid=Q712534|1=Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines}}. Tosetsha Shrine on the left, Saisetsha Shrine on the right. Both are cultural properties designated by Kyoto Prefecture. ]] {{ill|lt=Ryuzo|Q210684|qid=Q210684|lt=Ikkensha Ruzo|1=Nagare-zukuri}}{{ill|lt=杮葺|Q199388|qid=Q199388|1=Wood shingle}}. This building was rebuilt in 1897 by Hidemochi Koide, the lord of the Sonobe domain, and is the largest Ichigen shrine building not only in the Tanba region but also in Kyoto Prefecture. The paintings of rainbow beams and wooden noses are simpler than those of the same period, and are inherited from earlier traditional techniques. The gable decoration has double rainbow beams, and the large taiheizuka (taiheizuka) is decorated with a water stream shaped oigata (oigata) to create a highlight. There is also a style common to the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ryotan region|1=UNKNOWN}} that does not include rainbow beams. {{ill|lt=Carpenter|Q203605|qid=Q203605|1=Carpentry}} is from {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Banshu|1=UNKNOWN}}{{ill|lt=Kato District|Q1933120|qid=Q1933120|1=Katō District, Hyōgo}} Shima Village. . It has a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=covered house|1=UNKNOWN}} with gabled roof and thatched roof, and is a cultural property designated by Kyoto Prefecture, including the covered house. === Others === The worship hall was built in the early Showa period, and has a flat thatched roof with three beams and two beams. The previous worship hall was rebuilt at the same time as the main hall, and was a {{ill|lt=Irimoya-zukuri|Q855025|qid=Q855025|1=East Asian hip-and-gable roof}}, thatched-boarded, open-air building with one beam row and two girder rows, and was relocated to the precincts as an emasha (however, the roof was replaced with iron plates). The shrine gate was built by {{ill|lt=Hideaki Koide|Q11459127|qid=Q11459127|1=Hideaki Koide}} in {{ill|lt=Bunka (era name)|Q1373146|qid=Q1373146|lt=Bunka|1=Bunka}}5 ({{ill|lt=1808|Q6914|qid=Q6914|1=1808}}). The roof is made of copper sheets (previously it was thatched). The {{ill|lt=kumimono|Q7814068|qid=Q7814068|1=Tokyō (architecture)}} uses {{ill|lt=two-hands-gumi|UNKNOWN|lt=two-hands}} with tail rafters, the wooden nose is openworked, and the rainbow beams are carved with fancy wave patterns, showing the characteristics of Bunka period buildings. Kyoto Prefecture registered cultural property. The stone torii gate was built by Yoshihisa Koide in {{ill|lt=Kanbun|Q1146228|qid=Q1146228|1=Kanbun (era)}}12 ({{ill|lt=1672|Q7614|qid=Q7614|1=1672}}) and is a registered cultural property of Kyoto Prefecture. The Makibashi bridge that spans the approach to the shrine is also known as the ``Ichini Mabashi Bridge'' because visitors from the Sonobe clan were required to disembark their horses at the Makibashi bridge that spans the Sonobe River in front of the shrine. It is a simple structure with almost no decorations, {{ill|lt=gabled structure|Q13308575|qid=Q13308575|1=Kirizuma-style}}, and both have a 2-ken gable roof and a 2-ken girder, but the Tosetsu-sha has a 2-ken girder and the Sai-setsu-sha has a 3-ken length. Ryosetsusha was also rebuilt at the same time as the main shrine. Each has a gabled roofed roof with a flat thatched roof, and the roofed roof is designated as a cultural property by Kyoto Prefecture. * Saisetsha ** Deities enshrined: Kumano Shrine in Kuroda, Wakamiya Shrine in {{ill|lt=Yokota, Sonobe Town|Q131900099|qid=Q131900099|lt=Yokota|1=Yokota}}, |Miwa Shrine, Kamo Shrine in Omura, Shishi Sugahara Shrine, Handa Omori Shrine ** Enshrined on the right hand side facing the main shrine. See Tosetsha. * Shu Shrine * Kotohira Shrine * Sanno Shrine * Inari Shrine * {{ill|lt=Ise Jingu|Q687168|qid=Q687168|1=Ise Grand Shrine}} Far place of worship * Outside company ** {{ill|lt=Otabisho|Q11489117|qid=Q11489117|1=Otabisho}} ({{Wiki coordinates|35|6|22.93|N|135|26|20.23|E|region:JP|Yawata Shrine|name=Yawata Shrine ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Otabisho|1=UNKNOWN}})}}, Funasaka, Sonobe-cho, Nantan City) [https://tanbarakuichi.sakura.ne.jp/shrine/sonobe/04.html#s036 Hachiman Shrine] (Tamba Shrine [Personal Site]) Make-jinja otabisho.JPG|Otabisho (Hachiman Shrine) === Ritual organization === === Shinto priest === Engi's receipts suggest that a yubu was established during the Heian period, but the details are unknown. From the Middle Ages to the early modern period, Godaisan Takinji Temple was in charge as a Betto, and after the temple was abolished, the Ueda clan, a descendant of the Sonobe clan, took over the position of chief priest. === Miyaza === In each hamlet (village) of shrine parishioners, a group called ``Miyashu'' (Miyashu), which is made up of influential ``byo'' ({{ill|lt=surname|Q69634220|qid=Q69634220|lt=surname|1=myōji}}) of the clan group called ``kabu'', is organized, and they participate in festivals and perform their respective divine duties. In the case of Takei, the Miyamoto, one Miyashu is selected from each of the six specific families of the former {{ill|lt=Maki Village|Q30938084|qid=Q30938084|1=Make}} (term of six years). . From the other former Shinoda, Imai, and Tsujita families, eight specific families assumed the position of chief priest (kujuto, kunyuto). , assisting the chief priest in rituals, etc. The Miyaza of each of these villages is responsible for the rituals of the Moki Shrine, and at the same time is also involved in the rituals of the respective village ujigami, and there is a multilayered structure in which the rituals of the village ujigami and the rituals of the main ujigami, the Magi Shrine, are recognized. This multilayered structure of rituals is widely recognized in the Tamba region, and the rituals at Maki Shrine can be considered a typical example of this because of the breadth of the area and the preservation of the ancient style of Shinto rituals. ; Multilayered structure of ritualsFor example, in the case of Shimo-shin-e Village, there is a group of Okanae and 7 other members of the same family, and 5 of these members form the shrine sect called {{ill|lt=Toya|UNKNOWN|lt=Toya system}}, and at the same time they serve the Shinko Festival and are also responsible for the rituals of Hiruko Shrine, the village's guardian deity, which also overlaps with the rituals of the Kuta, which enshrines the ancestral deity. The Okabu family is said to be a descendant of a medieval {{ill|lt=jiji-samurai|Q13432011|qid=Q13432011|1=Jizamurai}}, and behind the main family's mansion there is a {{ill|lt=spring water|Q1881858|qid=Q1881858|1=spring water}} called ``Morisan Water'' and a small shrine called ``Jishu Daigongen'' enshrined as deities of the stock, which are the original ``guardian deities.'' Similarly, other stocks enshrined stock deities (mostly large trees) called ``Morisan'', ``Jigami'', and ``Yama no Kami'' on a per-plant basis, and together with other stocks, they formed shrines and took part in the rituals at Ebisu-jinja Shrine and Maki-jinja Shrine. In this way, each village in the ``Eleven Villages'' has three layers of overlapping rituals: ``Ushigami,'' ``Village Ujigami,'' and ``General Ujigami.'' Similarly, in Takei, which is a Miyamoto province, the Maki Shrine, which is the general guardian deity, is also regarded as the village guardian deity, but the rituals are divided into three parts: those of the ``village guardian deity'' and those of the ``general guardian deity.'' === Main festivals === === Rice planting festival === The rice-planting festival is a ritual to celebrate the fertility of {{ill|lt=Gokoku|Q1191138|qid=Q1191138|1=Five Grains}} of the Takei village, which represents the character of the deity enshrined at this shrine.In early modern times, it was held on May 5th ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Boys' Festival|1=UNKNOWN}}), but due to the calendar change, it was held on June 5th, and now it is held on the Sunday closest to June 5th. First, {{ill|lt=food for the gods|Q11591045|qid=Q11591045|1=Shinsen}} and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=rice cake|1=UNKNOWN}} were offered, and {{ill|lt=oryoto|Q1760119|qid=Q1760119|1=Norito}} was played, and then {{ill|lt=taiko|Q11404|qid=Q11404|1=Drum}} was placed in the shrine. {{ill|lt=Saotome|Q539854|qid=Q539854|1=Saotome}} wearing {{ill|lt=kasuri|Q3081545|qid=Q3081545|1=Kasuri}} of {{ill|lt=cotton|Q11457|qid=Q11457|1=Cotton}} of nk|indigo dye|Q11622590}} form a circle and dance the ``rice planting dance'' to the beat of the drum and songs. Next, the head of the shrine (see the previous section) holds a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=bamboo pole|1=UNKNOWN}} with a house-shaped board attached to the tip and a {{ill|lt=naruko (instrument)|UNKNOWN|lt=naruko}} suspended from it, as if it were a {{ill|lt=hoe|Q131154|qid=Q131154|1=Hoe (tool)}}, and performs the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=paddling|1=UNKNOWN}} gesture, using the stairs (5 steps) of the main shrine as a rice field. Afterwards, the two Saotomes are handed 25 sacred rice cakes by the chief priest, and each of them makes the gesture of planting five rice cakes on each step of the stairs, which are made to look like rice fields (the rice cakes are likened to seedlings). Next, the ``Rice Planting Dance'' is repeated, and when it is finished, Saotome collects the rice cakes she has planted and hands them over to the chief priest again, and the worshipers complete the ritual by offering {{ill|lt=Tamagushi|Q7680557|qid=Q7680557|1=Tamagushi}}.It is said that in ancient times, {{ill|lt=kagura|Q1348260|qid=Q1348260|1=Kagura}} was performed by {{ill|lt=priestess|Q1047139|qid=Q1047139|1=Miko}}, but the details are unknown. The current "rice planting dance" was created by the chief priest at the time in {{ill|lt=Showa|Q327567|qid=Q327567|1=Shōwa era}}9 ({{ill|lt=1934|Q18714|qid=Q18714|1=1934}})[http://www.bunkashisan.ne.jp/search/ViewContent.php?from=14&ContentID=135 Regional Cultural Asset Portal, ``Maki Shrine Rice Planting Festival''] (accessed October 26, 2010). The "Rice-planting Dance" was created in 1923 during {{ill|lt=Emperor Showa|Q34479|qid=Q34479|1=Hirohito}}'s {{ill|lt=Daijosai|Q11433653|qid=Q11433653|1=Daijosai}}. The song is said to have been written and choreographed based on the rice-planting ceremony that took place when the area around {{ill|lt=Ogami Shrine|Q11488762|qid=Q11488762|1=Mikami Shrine}} in 1358}} was designated as Yukida. , although it belongs to a new category, the rest remains well preserved. In addition, many women from the shrine parishioners participated in the "Rice Planting Dance", but that organization was disbanded in {{ill|lt=postwar|Q1201472|qid=Q1201472|1=Post-war}}, and in 1975 ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=1975|1=UNKNOWN}}), the number of women participating has decreased, so in August 1981, the God-Respecting Women's Association was formed to maintain and pass on the tradition, and since then, 10 to 15 people, mainly from the association, have been participating in the "Rice Planting Dance.". === Shinko Festival === The Shinko Festival is a festival of the 11 villages (11 shrines) of Makigo, and in early modern times, it was held from August {{ill|lt=last day|Q4704589|qid=Q4704589|1=misoka}} to September {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=first day|1=UNKNOWN}} along with the regular festival. Since Meiji 16 ({{ill|lt=1883|Q7816|qid=Q7816|1=1883}}), the Shinko Festival has been held on October 14th and 15th, but since {{ill|lt=Heisei|Q234510|qid=Q234510|1=Heisei era}} 15th year ({{ill|lt=2003|Q1986|qid=Q1986|1=2003}}), the Shinko Festival has been held on the third Saturday and Sunday of October. In the past, in addition to Miyamoto, parishioners from 9 villages and 11 companies participated, but currently the 4 villages of Kuroda, {{ill|lt=Yokota, Sonobe Town|Q131900099|qid=Q131900099|lt=Yokota|1=Yokota}}, Omura, and Kuchihatta do not participate. . ; the previous day On the day before the Shinko Festival, a shrine was set up in the gardens of the shrine inns set up in Funasaka and Nie.In the past, in Funasaka, the shrine was chosen from among the 12 designated families, and later from the house of the group on duty (in some cases, newly built houses were selected) (``Shikiuchisha Survey Report''). The chief priest of this shrine visits Funasaka, and the chief priest (see the previous section) visits Nie to prepare for the festival. ; 1st dayEarly on the morning of the day, two messengers from the Shishi people were sent to our shrine, and after a festival (Shishi people offering ceremony) was held where sake and {{ill|lt=edamame|Q1377879|qid=Q1377879|1=Edamame}} were offered, the shrine was again {{ill|lt=morning|Q55313888|qid=Q55313888|1=a.m.}}1 The festival begins at 0:00, and at 2:00 PM, the {{ill|lt=Mikoshi|Q979940|qid=Q979940|1=Mikoshi}} departs for {{ill|lt=Otabisho|Q11489117|qid=Q11489117|1=Otabisho}} in Funasaka, and the Shinko Festival begins. On the way, the mikoshi is greeted by a {{ill|lt=chigo|Q30940647|qid=Q30940647|1=Chigo}} procession from Nie and heads to Ebisu Shrine, where it is enshrined in the hall of worship and undergoes rituals by the head of the shrine and Nie's members of the shrine (see the previous section) before heading back to the otabisho. Then, a procession of Chigo from Funasaka joins them on the way, arrives at the Otabisho in the evening, the mikoshi is placed in a temporary hall set up at the Otabisho, and receives an offering of {{ill|lt=Tawara|Q11386402|qid=Q11386402|1=tawara}} containing fresh grain from Nie and Funasaka. Regarding Chigo, Nie is considered to be a female character, and Funasaka is considered to be a male character, and they are required to wear either female or male costumes. Until around 1932, a similar mikoshi was carried from Wakamiya Shrine in {{ill|lt=Yokota, Sonobe-machi|Q131900099|qid=Q131900099|lt=Yokota|1=Yokota}}, and people from Funasaka would meet them and accompany them to Otabisho, where the mikoshi of both Moki and Wakamiya shrines would be lined up and lodged together. ; 2nd dayIn the early hours of the next morning (around 2 a.m.), shrine parishioners including the Takei, Nie, Funasaka, Shishi, Onishi, and Handa shrines gather at the otabisho, where ``neri'' and dedications of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=sumo power|1=UNKNOWN}} are held. At this time, a person called Satanin, chosen from among the Shishi and Onishi, performs the ritual under the instructions of the chief priest.The Satanin of the Shishi is changed every other year, and the Satanin of the Onishi is changed every year. . First, the ritual begins with the command from the Sata people to ``offer the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=sacred sake|1=UNKNOWN}},'' and the worshipers chosen from Funasaka hold the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=sakaki|1=UNKNOWN}} in their mouths and bring two {{ill|lt=bottles|Q3129558|qid=Q3129558|1=heishi}} filled with the sacred sake to the shrine. Next, pour it into {{ill|lt=Choshi|Q2972145|qid=Q2972145|1=Chōshi}} and give it to the chief priest who attends the shrine. The priest who receives it refills it into another bottle and offers it, and the Choshi returns it to the donor. Next, when the Sataman commands, ``Drop the sacred sake,'' the chief priest pours the sacred sake from the bottle into the {{ill|lt=cup|Q3469363|qid=Q3469363|1=sakazuki}}, leaves it in front of the shrine, and returns the remaining sacred sake, along with the bottle, to the donor. Next, Satajin tells the chief priest, ``Come and enjoy the sacred sake,'' and together they go down to the gathering hall in the otabisho called ``Funasakacho,'' where they perform {{ill|lt=direct meeting|Q11581721|qid=Q11581721|1=Naorai}} with divine sake and a side dish made from cut {{ill|lt=persimmons|Q29526|qid=Q29526|1=Persimmon}}. Afterwards, the chief priest and Satato returned to the shrine again, and Satato ordered them to "stand for the offering," and the offeror gave two large {{ill|lt=笥|Q11600004|qid=Q11600004|1=ke}} offerings to the god. Eleven bowls and small bowls of sacred food are offered (the large bowl is said to be for the deity enshrined at this shrine, and the small bowl is said to be for the deity enshrined at the Setsusha (the deity enshrined at the Setsusha is also the deity enshrined at the 11 guardian deities of each village)), and the process begins. It is said that at the time when the mikoshi of Wakamiya Shrine lived together in the same lodging, the dedicator divided into two groups and carried the offerings to each mikoshi, and the shrine maiden from Wakamiya Shrine received the offerings and offered them to the mikoshi. Although it is now abbreviated, in the past, before the parade, the food was withdrawn with the signal of ``Sata-oroshi'' from the Sata people.The neri is also called ``doronai tori'' because of the way it is performed, and it is performed by Satato, Takei, and Handa's kakurikitori. The performer picks up a sword for one person, hangs a fish basket around his waist, and goes around the {{ill|lt=dohyō|Q832429|qid=Q832429|1=Dohyō}} set up in the Otabisho once.During this, he stabs the ground with his sword and says things like ``Ottaa'' while grabbing a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=doronago|1=UNKNOWN}} and making a gesture to put it in the fish basket. Afterwards, the head of the shrine calls for a sumo force, but first the actual action is performed, followed by what is called ``half sumo force.'' The fights are divided into ``Dekaku Riki'' and ``Machikaku Riki'', with the Kakuro Tori of the Machikaku Riki-ka going up to the ring first and receiving techniques from the Dekaku Riki-ka who comes up later, and the 7th match being held with the Dekaku Riki-ka playing the winning role and the Machikaku Riki-ka playing the losing role (however, there is no winner or loser). Half-force power is when one person performs the act of taking power (one-person power), and at the end, the person rolls around as if he has been thrown away. This represents the opponent of the rice spirit, an invisible god of energy, and by being thrown away by that god, it is said to be a blessing to the gods and a prayer for a bountiful harvest. Once the half-witness force is finished, Takei and Funasaka perform the training, and the ritual ends. It is customary for parishioners from 11 shrines to participate in the ceremony, and in the four villages that are not participating, members of Takei serve as substitutes to maintain the ancient status. Regarding the practice, it seems to be a remnant of the past negative attitude (Makewaza) associated with the power of power with the gods due to its humorous appearance, but it is considered to be a tradition that should be considered along with the ``Catfish Osame Shinto Ritual'' handed down at Ishigami Shrine in {{ill|lt=Hyogo Prefecture|Q130290|qid=Q130290|1=Hyōgo Prefecture}}.Around 2:00 pm on the second day of the Shinko Festival, the parishioners gather together bringing items such as straw bags, {{ill|lt=bow and arrows|Q19827042|qid=Q19827042|1=Bow and arrow}}, targets, {{ill|lt=floor boxes|Q11485954|qid=Q11485954|1=Shogi}}, and orihito. First, the people from Funasaka offered bales and orihito to the mikoshi, and after singing prayers, Nie and Funasaka's party, led by Satato, offered {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=bundles|1=UNKNOWN}}, bows, targets, bales, orihito, etc., and the Shishi and Onishi on duty {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=plow|1=UNKNOWN}} - Two {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=machiko|1=UNKNOWN}} {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=cow|1=UNKNOWN}} carrying {{ill|lt=horse hoe|Q209042|qid=Q209042|1=Harrow (tool)}} follow in a single line and circle around the Funasaka Office three times in a thousand degrees. At the end of Osendo, children from Nie and Funasaka wave bundles of money in front of the mikoshi (hohei), and then a Yabusame ceremony is held in which they ride on {{ill|lt=wooden horse|Q647794|qid=Q647794|1=Rocking horse}} and shoot arrows at targets held up by the target bearer.Yabusame used to be held early in the morning (``Shikinaisha Investigation Report''). . Once Yabusame is over, the mikoshi is returned to the shrine. After Kanko left the Otabisho, everyone other than Takei and Nie saw the mikoshi off to Sasayama Kaido, and Nie's group accompanied him to the vicinity of Nie's community center. When the mikoshi returns to Maki Shrine in the evening, the festival ends by carrying it around the shrine, shaking it vigorously up and down. Furthermore, until 1962 (1962|Q2764}}), mikoshis were carried on pilgrimages, but due to the decrease in the number of people carrying them, they are now carried on carts. === Cultural assets === === Cultural property designated by Kyoto Prefecture === *Tangible cultural property ** Maki Shrine 3 buildings (buildings) - Designated on April 14, 1984 [http://www.kyoto-be.ne.jp/bunkazai/cms/?page_id=200 Kyoto Prefecture designated/registered cultural properties] (Kyoto Prefecture Board of Education). . *** Main shrine *** Tosetsha *** Saisetsha *** (Designated) 3 covered houses === Kyoto prefecture registered cultural property === *Tangible cultural property ** Maki Shrine 3 buildings (buildings) - Registered on April 14, 1984. *** Emasha *** Shinmon *** Torii === Kyoto Prefecture Cultural Properties Environmental Conservation District === * Maki Shrine Cultural Properties Environmental Conservation District - Decided on April 14, 1984. === Cultural property designated by Nantan City === * Natural monument ** Tengu cedar at the mouth of Maki Shrine - Designated on April 13, 2017 {{PDFlink|[http://www.be.city.nantan.kyoto.jp/syakaikyouiku/bunkazai29.6.8.pdf Nantan City Cultural Properties List]}} (Nantan City homepage). . === Local information === ; Location * {{ill|lt=Kyoto Prefecture|Q120730|qid=Q120730|1=Kyoto Prefecture}}{{ill|lt=Nantan City|Q170421|qid=Q170421|1=Nantan, Kyoto}}3 Takei Miyanoya, Sonobe Town ; Transportation access * bus ** {{ill|lt=Sonobe Station|Q1044120|qid=Q1044120|1=Sonobe Station}} ({{ill|lt=West Japan Railway Company|Q502125|qid=Q502125|lt=JR West|1=West Japan Railway Company}}{{ill|lt=Sagano Line|Q1073011|qid=Q1073011|1=Sagano Line}}/{{ill|lt=San'in Main Line|Q1135170|qid=Q1135170|1=San'in Main Line}}), take the Nantan Municipal Bus (44 Enshino Line) and get off at the "Makijinja-mae" bus stop.
